papers.title: BQ-LoRA: Binary-Quantized Low-Rank Adapters as Implicit Regularizers for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of quantized large language models is dominated by QLoRA, which combines 4-bit weight quantization with FP16 low-rank adapters. We ask whether the FP16 adapter precision is necessary. Replacing it with a single binary bit per adapter parameter, combined with a learned per-layer scale $s$ and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, reduces adapter storage by 13-16x. We introduce two variants -- NormScale, which binarizes under a norm-preserving scale with a clipped STE, and LearnThresh, which makes the binarization threshold learnable -- unified under a framework we call BQ-LoRA. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight characterization of the BQ-LoRA hypothesis class: it has bounded entrywise norm, a typical-set spectral norm bound that is $Θ(r)$ times sharper than the worst case, a full-rank, near-isotropic update, and consequently a Rademacher complexity that yields an explicit $\tilde{O}(s_{\max}α\sqrt{d_{out}/(rn)})$ generalization bound. FP16 LoRA has no comparable a priori norm or isotropy control. On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA exceeds QLoRA's benchmark averages at every scale by 0.8-3.5 points; on LLaMA-2 (7B/70B) it remains competitive at the same storage reduction but does not uniformly lead the strongest FP16-adapter baselines (LoftQ at 7B, QLoRA at 70B). On Qwen2.5-7B the binary adapter preserves the 4-bit base WikiText-2 PPL within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80) while QLoRA worsens it by 0.59. The reduction applies to inference-time adapter storage and serving; training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%. We translate the storage saving into a deployment study, BQ-SGMV, by extending Punica's SGMV kernel with a binary inner-product primitive: the same A100-80GB holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM, and our research prototype eliminates cache misses under a skewed synthetic workload.

papers.title: M$^3$-Test: Coverage Gaps in Joint-Perturbation Testing of Visual Question Answering
papers.abstract: A visual question answering (VQA) model can pass every image-only and question-only test yet fail when the same changes occur together. Standard robustness reports average over conditions and therefore cannot say which accepted requests remain vulnerable. We introduce M3-Test, a coverage audit that aligns each clean input with its single-modality variants and a complete 5x5 family, 4x4 strength joint library, so that any reduced test suite can be replayed on the same requests. Across 2.6 million responses from four vision-language models, joint failures affect 26-29% of the Qwen questions that pass all 40 single-modality tests, although fewer than 0.6% of their joint records fail. Passing the 25 maximum-strength corners does not close this gap: 11-14% of the accepted questions still fail elsewhere in the library. Re-executing the archived failures reproduces about 90% of them, against a 0.3-0.6% flip rate among matched passing controls, and re-checking the most fragile failure records supports 80-89% of them. On the evidence examined, neither execution noise nor grading error can fully account for the gap. The same aligned grids make previous evaluations reusable. On held-out images, a risk order learned from other models discovers about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 additional queries, compared with 65-68% for maximum-first and 53-57% for pairwise covering arrays. M3-Test thus turns a passing robustness suite into a request-level account of what remains untested, supporting acceptance, regression review and test allocation.

papers.title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. Our interpretability experiments suggest that VRLLM learns feature-specific predictive associations, while component ablations indicate that the earliest two FFN layers contribute to the emergence of linearly decodable task information. Our paper provides an engineering recipe and a focused empirical case study on adapting compact LLMs to industrial tabular prediction tasks.

papers.title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
papers.abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce OAK-Mind, a zerO-training, multi-Agent, Knowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

papers.title: VTT: Reading Vehicle Size and Powertrain Type from Motion Trajectory Across Unseen Car Models
papers.abstract: Vehicle size and powertrain information can enrich trajectory data for traffic analysis and simulation. We present VTT, a dataset and benchmark for identifying these attributes from motion and controller area network (CAN) signals across unseen car models. The dataset contains 9,062 drives, about 3,950 h, from 1,431 vehicles and 174 car models. It provides three footprint-based size classes, powertrain labels, and evaluation on unseen car models and unseen drivers. Using 60-s windows, we compare four sequence architectures, statistical features and physical features proposed by large language models. Training with auxiliary physical targets, data augmentation and task-specific weighting raises drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion vehicles and from 62.9% to 67.1% for size classification. On public logs from 4,061 additional drivers, the full-input model identifies powertrain correctly for 86 of 88 car models; size accuracy is 63.2%, close to the internal vehicle-level result of 63.5%. Physical-feature analysis links powertrain recognition to deceleration behaviour and size recognition to steering response. Errors near size-class boundaries and limited gains from longer observations highlight the importance of label resolution and training-fleet coverage for cross-model generalisation.

papers.title: Latent Lattice Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.

papers.title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters
papers.abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.

papers.title: BLIP-Live: Balancing Timeliness & Firing Precision in Proactive Streaming Video Agents
papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.

papers.title: TRACK: Tool-Augmented Reasoning over Time Series for Fault Diagnosis in Power Management System
papers.abstract: Fault diagnosis in power management systems running multiple loads relies on experts manually inspecting current and voltage waveforms, which fails to scale across deployed units. We present TRACK, which pairs a time series encoder with a Small Language Model to produce structured, physics-grounded diagnostic reports, calling tools for exact, verifiable calculations. It operates on-device, keeping proprietary sensor data local and avoiding expensive API calls. We introduce a rubric-based framework that evaluates these reports by scoring structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability through per-criterion verdicts. On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, TRACK achieves over 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, whereas the best encoder-probing baseline reaches only 58% accuracy.

papers.title: CivilBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Information Integration in Civil Engineering
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/traceuryuan/CivilBench.

papers.title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models
papers.abstract: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/

papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

papers.title: GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model
papers.abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are widely used for step-level evaluation of multi-step reasoning in large language models, but existing methods are often limited by weak historical dependency modeling and insufficient global awareness. They typically fail to leverage prior step evaluations for coherent judgment and lack visibility into subsequent reasoning, leading to suboptimal assessment of intermediate steps. To address this issue, we propose the Global Perspective Process Reward Model (GPRM), which jointly models the problem, previous reasoning steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps to enable history-aware and globally informed process evaluation. We further introduce a structured evaluation framework along four dimensions---look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment---to assess prior consistency, future plausibility, step validity, and task alignment. Based on this framework, we construct datasets for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Experiments show that, despite using less training data and smaller model sizes, GPRM outperforms strong baseline models by 7.8 and 5.4 points on PRMBench and ProcessBench, respectively. GPRM also generalizes well across tasks, surpassing the GPT-4.1 baseline on Agent Error Bench, improving strong baselines by around 4 points under test-time scaling (TTS), and achieving competitive performance on PPE.

papers.title: Competent Autonomous Driving Through Fine Tuning Vision Language Action Models with Symbolic Traffic Rules
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a unified approach to perception, reasoning, and control for autonomous driving, but accurate action prediction alone does not establish compliance with traffic regulations. This paper presents a rule-guided VLA framework that incorporates symbolic traffic-rule feedback into policy optimisation. The framework combines supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations with reinforcement learning (RL) refinement using a reward that encourages encoded-rule compliance while penalising deviations from expert actions. Selected provisions of the United Kingdom Highway Code are formalised as executable first-order logic rules using PyReason, covering speed adaptation, following distance, and road-user priority. A frozen vision-language model extracts scene predicates, which are combined with vehicle-state information to assess the projected consequences of candidate control actions. Offline evaluation on held-out data collected in the CARLA simulator compares three group-based RL methods. The results show improvements in both action prediction accuracy and encoded-rule compliance over the supervised baseline. The best-performing variant increases the overall rule pass rate from 92.9% to 97.6%, with zero observed violations of the encoded road-user-priority check in the evaluated samples. These findings support symbolic rule feedback as a means of improving VLA policy alignment with explicit traffic-rule criteria.

papers.title: Necessary for What? Auditing Demographic Disclosure to LLM Synthetic Respondents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly answer surveys on behalf of real panelists, and each panelist's recorded demographic attributes (e.g., age, education, ethnicity) are often placed in the prompt on the premise that richer profiles make more faithful synthetic respondents. While data minimization limits personal data to what a purpose requires, a synthetic survey serves several purposes at once, from predicting individual answers to estimating how opinions are distributed and comparing groups. We ask which of these purposes require the respondent's record, and whether improved estimates support sound conclusions about groups. We vary whose profile a model receives, where it comes from, and how many fields it contains, in two U.S. surveys with eleven open-weight and three hosted models, and compare each model with a statistical model fit to the same information. We make four contributions. First, we show that the record adds little to individual predictions and that, for the open-weight models, most of its gain in population estimates remains when it is replaced by census data or a synthetic persona. Second, we find that group comparisons improve only with the respondent's own record, and that even then the models' group differences rest more on the demographic label in the prompt than on the individual respondent, which the usual check of reproducing known group differences does not reveal. Third, we find that the models make groups look more alike than they are, keeping differences in circumstances while flattening or reversing differences in attitudes, most sharply for religious affiliation and ethnic origin, both special categories of personal data. Fourth, we outline an audit that a survey organization can run on questions it has already fielded to decide which estimates may use the record.

papers.title: LEDGE: Separating Critic and Editor Failures in Text-to-Image Self-Correction
papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) self-correction combines a vision-language model (VLM) critic that diagnoses errors and proposes instructions with an image editor that executes them. End-to-end evaluation obscures whether failures arise from incorrect diagnoses or an editor unable to execute valid instructions. We introduce LEDGE (Learning Error Diagnosis in Generation and Editing), a framework that separates these bottlenecks. LEDGE compiles oracle edit instructions from GenEval while holding the generated images and the editor fixed, isolating the editor's correction capability from the critic's diagnostic accuracy. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large, oracle instructions raise GenEval from 72.0% to 81.2%, versus 74.1% for the baseline VLM critic. Yet 435 of 644 failed images remain unrepaired, exposing a substantial editor gap. We also use oracle labels from disjoint training prompts to supervise the critic. Oracle supervision raises exact diagnosis from 33.3% (the same VLM with our structured output, untrained) to 70.8%. With the same editor, the resulting critic improves GenEval from 42.2% (uncorrected) to 59.4% on Stable Diffusion 1.5, against 50.9% for the baseline critic, and from 72.0% to 76.0% on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large, despite training only on Stable Diffusion 1.5. Improvements transfer to unseen object classes, a second editor, and independent T2I-CompBench judges and prompts. A small human evaluation confirms the ranking in estimated net corrections but suggests a smaller gain than detector-based evaluation. LEDGE thus distinguishes two limits of self-correction: knowing what to fix and being able to fix it.

papers.title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
papers.abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 75% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 40%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 80-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

papers.title: Self-supervised learning for zebrafish embryo phenotype evaluation: Systematic comparison of algorithms, label-efficient classification, and transfer learning
papers.abstract: Zebrafish embryos are a prominent model organism for image-based phenotyping and especially suited for large-scale imaging studies, for which machine learning (ML) models can automate evaluation. However, training ML models usually requires large labeled datasets, and differences in imaging conditions often impede reuse across laboratories. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses both constraints by learning transferable representations from unlabeled images. Yet central aspects like the choice of algorithm remain underexplored for domain-specific applications. To close this gap, we benchmark popular SSL algorithms on the public EmbryoNet dataset, explore label-efficient learning, and test transfer to an unseen setting. Using representations from our strongest model, a ResNet50 network trained with SwAV, a simple linear classifier reaches 86.4% accuracy and a non-linear classifier 87.1%, rivaling the fully supervised EmbryoNet model (87.1%). The SwAV model decisively outperforms supervised training from scratch when labels are scarce (70.2% vs. 45.7% accuracy with 5% of labels). On a three-class problem (normal, dead, falsely cropped) with a small, previously unseen zebrafish toxicity dataset, recorded in a different setting, our model reaches 81.3% accuracy without retraining, while EmbryoNet achieves 75.9%. Overall, self-supervised models for zebrafish embryos seem to mostly facilitate label-efficiency and transfer to new settings rather than improving supervised results.

papers.title: GNN-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Coastal Emergency Response under Extreme Water Levels
papers.abstract: When a storm surge approaches a coastal town, the emergency plan must be put into action quickly using water-level forecasts, flood extent, road access, vulnerable residents and shelters. Bringing this information together under time pressure is slow and depends on the duty officer's expertise. This paper is one step in a wider research line from data to safe decisions: machine learning to understand the hazard, reinforcement learning and planning to choose actions, large language models (LLMs) to explain and cross-check them, and an assurance layer that keeps people in charge. Here we address the action step on a real place. We ask whether a policy can learn the timing of emergency actions from decades of real events. Lido di Venezia is represented as a heterogeneous graph built from public elevation, road, building and census data and driven by hourly tide-gauge records from 1983 to 2024, with seven actions taken from the municipal emergency plan. A PPO policy is trained on this graph and compared, on storm windows unseen in training, with a rule-based system simulating the officer's discretionary decisions. On 18 historical test scenarios, PPO achieves a similar reduction in population exposure to the rule. With uncertain forecasts and limited protection it again performs similarly but does not outperform the tuned rule, and removing graph message passing does not substantially reduce performance. PPO therefore learns an effective protective response from an outcome-based reward alone: it is given the plan's actions and when each is allowed, but not the thresholds that tell the comparator when to act. Next steps test harder edge cases, move closer to a digital twin of the territory, and replace the simulated officer with assessment by emergency-management stakeholders, supported by LLM-based interpretation of each recommendation.

papers.title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.

papers.title: Can decision models extract clinical data from cancer pathology reports? An evaluation of accuracy, calibration, and failure modes
papers.abstract: Decision models are a new class of language model that, instead of generating text, choose one option per question from a fixed list and return a probability for every option. They have not yet been evaluated on clinical text. We evaluated two open-weights decision models, Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B, for extracting 25 fields from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports from a single centre, against a prospectively maintained clinical database. We compared them with two generative models: Qwen3.5 9B, run locally, and GLM-5.3-flash, run through a cloud API. Tev1 reached a mean field accuracy of 0.917 (95% CI 0.913 to 0.920), the same as Qwen3.5 9B (0.918; p = 0.26), and was four times faster (15 s against 61 s per report). Nimble reached 0.862 and GLM-5.3-flash 0.986. Both decision models matched GLM-5.3-flash on simple dichotomous categories. They were weak on measurements binned into categories, on fields whose correct answer was not reported, and on some complex decisions (e.g. involved margins). We found that the main cause of the inferior performance of Nimble's came from asking 25 questions in one request: with two questions per request, its accuracy improved. Pooled over fields, the returned probabilities were well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.022 and 0.026), but they did not flag systematic errors within single fields. A simulated strategy of sending answers with a probability below 0.94 to GLM-5.3-flash raised Tev1's accuracy to 0.982, with 38% of answers escalated. Decision models can extract explicitly stated findings from pathology reports quickly on local hardware and return useful probabilities. They should be validated in the configuration in which they will be used, restricted to the fields in which they are reliable, and combined with other methods for numeric values.

papers.title: A Corpus-Driven SentencePiece Unigram Tokenizer for Sindhi: Design and Benchmark Against Fourteen Existing Tokenizers
papers.abstract: Sindhi is a low-resource Indo-Aryan language written mainly in an extended Perso-Arabic script. Several Sindhi tokenizers have been released on public model hubs, but they have not been compared with one another on shared data. We train SentencePiece Unigram tokenizers with byte fallback at four vocabulary sizes (32k to 150k) on about 1.10 million Sindhi sentences and a smaller, repeated Urdu, Persian and Arabic slice, from four public sources, and compare them with fourteen existing tokenizers on four evaluation sets: FLORES+, Sindhi Wikipedia, a news-derived sentiment corpus, and a contemporary news corpus. The metrics are fertility, single-token retention, UNK rate, byte-fallback rate, and round-trip character loss. At 64k, our tokenizer averages 1.147 tokens per word, against 1.208 for the best existing tokenizer and 1.512 for XLM-RoBERTa, and keeps 88.6% of words as single tokens. On fertility, single-token retention and UNK rate it is best or tied for best in all four evaluation sets at 64k and above; at 32k it trails one baseline on FLORES+. Margins over the best Sindhi-adapted baselines are small (0.002 fertility on FLORES+ at 64k), and we report no significance tests. A round-trip check finds no character loss for our tokenizer and silent character deletion (up to 0.85% of characters) in two existing ones; seven others lose less than 0.1%. We evaluate intrinsic metrics only, so effects on downstream tasks remain untested. Code and tokenizer files are public (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23962474).

papers.title: Learning When to Continue and When to Stop: Termination-Aware OPSD
papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves language model reasoning by distilling from a frozen teacher initialized identically to the student and conditioned on privileged information. However, we identify an underexplored termination mismatch in OPSD: the student fails to reliably learn when to continue and when to stop. This mismatch manifests in two opposing failure modes-premature termination, where reasoning stops before sufficient progress is made, and repetition-driven over-generation, where the model continues generating after reasoning has stalled. Our analysis shows that the teacher-student discrepancy on EOS grows during OPSD training, while length-capped trajectories are frequently dominated by unproductive repetition. To address this issue, we propose TA-OPSD (Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation), which augments the original OPSD objective with two targeted objectives. Stop/Continue Distillation addresses premature termination by explicitly aligning the teacher and student on whether reasoning should continue, while Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training addresses repetition-driven over-generation by discouraging repetitive continuations in the student's failed trajectories. The resulting objective improves termination behavior from complementary directions: continuing when further reasoning is needed and stopping when reasoning becomes unproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 (1.7B/4B/8B) show that TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all three model scales. Beyond the performance gains, ablation and behavioral analyses show that the two proposed objectives effectively mitigate their corresponding termination failures, reducing both premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation.

papers.title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over $π_{0.5}$) at 92.7 ms latency.

papers.title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
papers.abstract: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks. These findings indicate that LLM-derived embeddings do not uniformly improve Indic sentence similarity over established encoders and motivate evaluation that accounts for language coverage, task supervision, and benchmark construction.

papers.title: From zero-target transfer to target-site personalization: multi-source training across fall-detection models
papers.abstract: Video-based fall detection could support timely assistance when a person cannot call for help. Unfamiliar cameras and scarce local labels challenge deployment. We examine whether joint training improves cross-dataset detection and subsequent local training. We analyze 2,697 clips from eight OmniFall datasets and one AI-Hub dataset. Positive clips contain a fall or collapse transition, while negative clips do not. We hold out each dataset in turn, training on the other eight. We evaluate three vision-language models (VLMs), Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL, and three visual baselines, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. We evaluate the stored source model without target data for training or selection. For each label budget, we update a separate copy using labeled clips from the held-out target dataset. We call this target-site personalization. We compare the Source-initialized model with Target-only, which skips source training but uses identical target clips and updates. Across nine targets, source training raises mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from frozen-model values of 0.821 to 0.912 for Qwen, 0.883 to 0.947 for LLaVA, and 0.939 to 0.962 for InternVL. With five target examples per class and 26 updates per run, 95% confidence intervals for the AUROC benefit over Target-only lie above zero for Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. With full-target training, they lie above zero only for Qwen and LLaVA. Separate VLM analyses reveal threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections. The benefit varies by model and label budget.

papers.title: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live
papers.abstract: A voice agent that negotiates by phone must answer quickly, understand spoken amounts and cope with a caller who talks over it. We compared three architectures for such an agent, negotiating freight rates in Spanish: two cascades (speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis) orchestrated by Pipecat and by LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live, an OpenAI speech model that listens and speaks without separate stages. A program played the carrier with the same 47 recordings of one speaker for all agents, without the telephone network, in 77 calls per architecture over five negotiation scenarios, and measured latency on the listener's side with a validated instrument. Median latency to the content response was 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit) and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live); the confidence interval of GPT-Live's 171.2 ms advantage over Pipecat includes zero. According to its own timestamps, GPT-Live began to answer 800 ms after the end of the line, close to the 0.8 s published by OpenAI; most of the remaining wait, about 1,367 ms and nearly constant, is the audio's round trip through OpenAI's service. A tool call added 0.9-1.1 s in every architecture, more than any difference between them, and the frameworks' self-reported latency fell short of the listener's wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit). Word error rates were low (6.03, 4.93 and 1.47%), but the error on amounts was 13.01% and 12.61% in the cascades, against 2.86% in GPT-Live. With default settings, Pipecat and LiveKit stopped at almost every backchannel and often took it as the carrier's answer: an "ok" spoken over the agent ended in a registered agreement in 3 of 15 Pipecat calls, 2 of 15 LiveKit calls and no GPT-Live call (descriptive counts, not tested). Latency should therefore be measured on the listener's side, and a cascade needs safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannels.

papers.title: FiReIQ: Field-Level Confidence Estimation with Reasoning and Image Quality in Document Extraction
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in structured document extraction, yet their deployment in high-stakes applications requires reliable confidence estimates for individual fields. Existing uncertainty estimators often aggregate signals across an entire generation, obscuring field-specific reasoning uncertainty while overlooking visual degradations that may lead to confident extraction errors. To address these limitations, we introduce FiReIQ, a field-level confidence estimation framework that combines field-aligned reasoning signals from a single VLM generation with local and global image-quality features through quality-conditioned visual fusion. To facilitate systematic evaluation, we further introduce FiReIQ-Bench, a benchmark spanning financial receipts and legal contracts. Experiments with two reasoning VLMs show that FiReIQ consistently improves confidence discrimination, selective prediction, and probabilistic accuracy over existing estimators. These gains extend to private financial service data, where FiReIQ improves AUROC by 6.8% and coverage at 95% precision by 10.6% over an existing baseline. Together, these results highlight the potential of FiReIQ to reduce manual review while enabling more reliable document automation.

papers.title: Clean Tickets, Wrong Orders: Catching Silent Errors with a Language Model in Your Browser Tab
papers.abstract: A small language model that turns a typed order into structure can fail in two ways. It can print something broken, which any system rejects. Or it can print a clean, well formed order that nobody placed. Our companion work calls the second kind a silent error, and it is the dangerous one. We present a web demo in which a fine-tuned 0.8B parameter model runs entirely inside the visitor's browser tab, through llama.cpp compiled to WebAssembly. No order text leaves the device. The page parses orders as the visitor types, scores every ticket with the PIZZA benchmark's own matcher ported to TypeScript, refuses anything off the menu with "?" so the model can face the open web, and lets visitors hunt for silent errors or try to cause one. Run in the browser on all 1,357 PIZZA test orders, the deployed model writes the same output as the server evaluation for 99.0% of them and reaches the same exact match (0.882); we also report its latency on 3 consumer laptops. Demo: https://wrong.cuyor.com

papers.title: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents
papers.abstract: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. However, existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover only a small number of web applications drawn from a few software categories, and restrict modality to text and vision. Live benchmarks broaden site coverage but sacrifice reproducibility, since pages and data drift between runs. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not meaningfully evaluate whether agents can understand and use audio and video content embedded within web tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce WebArena-Pro, a benchmark comprising 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, spanning distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. Across the evaluated agents, the best performance is achieved by both Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. The strongest GenericAgent configurations, Gemini 3.1 Pro omni and Gemma4 31B, both achieve 30.3%. Among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks, WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and the most comprehensive multimodal support to date. The benchmark treats audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, with dedicated actions for extracting information from each. WebArena-Pro runs each task in isolation and supports reproducible, parallel evaluation. Tasks are authored through a dedicated annotator interface, filtered by LLM-assisted triage, and finally validated by humans before release. Project page: https://webarena-pro.github.io

papers.title: Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining
papers.abstract: A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends yet reduce it at the final training budget. We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal.

papers.title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLMs
papers.abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.

papers.title: UAV-Flow++: A Unified Suite for Benchmarking and Learning Language-Guided UAV Flight
papers.abstract: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.

papers.title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
papers.abstract: Structured Electronic Health Record (EHR) models typically represent clinical concepts as dataset-specific tokens, discarding their associated natural-language semantics. Consequently, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence without directly exploiting pretrained linguistic knowledge. We investigate the contribution of pretrained language semantics to longitudinal EHR prediction through tEHR, a framework that converts clinical events into natural-language descriptions and adapts pretrained autoregressive language models through EHR-specific continued pretraining and task-specific discriminative fine-tuning. We evaluate tEHR across four MIMIC-IV prediction tasks, where Mistral-7B achieves the strongest overall performance against structured-data, code-based, and LLM-based baselines. Controlled ablations demonstrate the importance of lexical grounding, numerical values, and both adaptation stages. A capacity-controlled experiment further shows that replacing clinical descriptions with atomic code tokens substantially reduces performance despite retaining the same LLM backbone. Alternative approaches incorporating pretrained semantic embeddings offer lower computational costs but do not match full textualisation. These results highlight the importance of both semantic representation and downstream adaptation when applying pretrained language models to structured EHR prediction.

papers.title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.

papers.title: Recursive State-Augmented Language Models: Persistent Latent-State Adaptation of Pretrained Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models rely on finite token contexts, limiting access to earlier interactions. We introduce Recursive State-Augmented Language Models (Recursive SALM), a framework in which a persistent latent state evolves with each observation and generates adaptations of a pretrained language model. A modular read-transition-write architecture separates observation encoding, latent dynamics, and predictor adaptation. We develop deterministic and stochastic formulations. The experiments evaluate only deterministic SALM with frozen GPT-2 small and exclude earlier evidence from its decoder context. On a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, latent-gated LoRA reaches 89.1% accuracy, comparable to 88.0% for a trained full-context LoRA baseline, with earlier evidence available solely through a 64-dimensional state. Zeroing or shuffling the state substantially reduces accuracy. In a two-turn task with codewords unseen in training, several interfaces improve candidate ranking over chance, but rarely generate the exact codeword under the evaluated training schedule. These experiments show that persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when earlier evidence is absent from the decoder context.

papers.title: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as primary interfaces for factual retrieval, yet current evaluation paradigms rely almost exclusively on explicit entity names. In this work, we demonstrate that LLM knowledge is fundamentally lexically anchored: models possess extensive factual information but find it significantly difficult to retrieve without explicit name tokens. To quantify this limitation, we introduce ShadowBench, a rigorously hardened, shortcut-resistant benchmark designed to evaluate Latent Entity Association via a novel Dual-Trait Association (DTA) task. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive "Shadow Gap" across all model scales$\unicode{x2013}$up to the frontier models GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6$\unicode{x2013}$where removing lexical anchors causes performance drops of over 20%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this lexical dependency exposes a critical vulnerability in AI safety. Applying ShadowBench to Machine Unlearning, we find that state-of-the-art algorithms (e.g., Gradient Difference, NPO) achieve only superficial lexical erasure. While unlearned models fail on direct queries, our novel Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) metric reveals that for popular entities, models explicitly reconstruct the "forgotten" entity in their internal reasoning traces in over 74% of cases, utilizing residual shadow knowledge to solve associative tasks. Conversely, for niche entities, models retain high shadow accuracy (60-90%) via implicit attribute correlation despite 0% LELR. Ultimately, ShadowBench indicates that current unlearning paradigms create an "Illusion of Forgetting," demonstrating that existing methods act as superficial output filters and are not yet reliable for achieving true parametric erasure.

papers.title: Curiosity-0826-4B: Generative Medical Event Sequence Modeling Across Pediatric and Adult Populations
papers.abstract: We introduce Curiosity-0826-4B, an updated version of the generative medical event foundation model trained on Epic Cosmos that simulates patient timelines to produce zero-shot clinical predictions. Curiosity-0826-4B incorporates a broader patient population and richer clinical event representations, while generally matching or exceeding Curiosity-0226-1B, the largest model in the previous Curiosity-0226 series, on evaluated tasks supported by both models. Laboratory value prediction improved, with MAE 18--46% lower than that of Curiosity-0226-1B. We evaluated prediction of disease events across pediatric cohorts aged 2--17 years. AUROCs for new asthma diagnosis (0.742--0.785) and asthma exacerbation (0.829--0.852) were comparable to those in the adult reference cohort, while AUROCs for sickle cell crisis (0.820--0.847) were lower than in adults (0.915). Explicit representation of documented death enabled new mortality prediction tasks among adults across hospice, inpatient, and ambulatory settings (AUROC 0.821--0.942). Scaling-law analysis guided compute-optimal initial pretraining followed by continued pretraining with context extension. The resulting Curiosity-0826-4B model has more parameters (4.3B versus 1B) and a longer context window (16K versus 8K). It processes 56% fewer training tokens and requires 2.2 times the training floating point operations (FLOPs) compared with its predecessor. By extending a common zero-shot prediction strategy to pediatric patients and additional outcomes, Curiosity-0826-4B broadens opportunities to develop clinical and operational applications without training separate task-specific models. Further validation should assess local calibration, performance across patient subgroups and event frequencies, timeline completion rates, and generalization to new settings, alongside prospective evaluation of clinical and operational utility.

papers.title: Differential Backpack Language Models: Sense Inhibition via Signed Contextualization Weights
papers.abstract: Backpack language models predict with a strictly linear combination of non-contextual per-word sense vectors, weighted by non-negative contextualization scores. We show that non-negativity conflates two properties: the linear readout, which carries the interpretability, and the conic combination, which merely restricts it. We relax the latter by computing the sense weights with differential attention, a difference of two softmax maps with a learned per-sense gain, so context can actively inhibit a sense; we call the result a differential Backpack. At equal parameters on WikiText-103 this cuts the Backpack's perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31%, improves over the softmax Backpack at every sense count, persists with a shrinking margin up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText, and is localized at the sense layer by ablations and controls. The learned inhibition is directly interpretable (a financial context drives the river sense of bank to -0.50), and the preserved per-sense attribution predicts counterfactual removals exactly. We tested a number of combination rules, showing the linear interface is nearly free. Making the readout nonlinear gains only 0.43 perplexity points while invalidating two thirds of the decomposition. The differential Backpack's senses are also better representations, improving zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.

papers.title: BiPOP: Partial-Order Planning for Long-Horizon Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Bimanual robotic manipulation is versatile, yet its central challenge lies not only in executing dexterous motion with each hand, but also in coordinating the two arms for long-horizon manipulation under coupled spatial and temporal constraints. Prior work has largely focused on endowing robots with human-level manipulation skills, paying less attention to the structure of bimanual behaviour itself: many practical tasks are a coordinated composition of reusable unimanual skills and a small set of synchronous bimanual skills. This makes high-level spatio-temporal coordination, rather than skill acquisition alone, a key bottleneck for efficient bimanual execution. We propose BiPOP, a framework that couples Large Language Models (LLMs) with Temporal Partial-Order Planning for long-horizon bimanual manipulation. At its core is an explicit spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and captures inter-arm dependencies, arm assignment, synchronization requirements, and opportunities for safe concurrent execution. Building on this model, an LLM translates natural-language instructions into a formal PDDL specification, while a temporal planner enforces the constraints and schedules actions, yielding plans that are logically consistent at the symbolic level and efficient through parallel execution. On simulated long-horizon tasks of varying complexity, BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with strong reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency, and the full pipeline runs end to end on the real bimanual robot NICOL. A failure analysis further shows that LLM-only planners mainly violate spatial and temporal coordination constraints, which motivates delegating these constraints to a symbolic planner. Code: https://github.com/Kchu/BiPOP

papers.title: AROMA: Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation for Vision-Language Model Control
papers.abstract: Mechanistic localization does not by itself yield usable control: causal sensitivity may occupy little activation energy, an accurate local direction may fail at finite scale, and a reachable numeral target may be wrong. We introduce AROMA (Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation), a frozen-VLM control framework separating where to intervene, which geometry and gain to use, how to reach a target, which target to pursue, and when to act. In Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, four dimensions of a causally validated cross-attention head explain 89.82% of cardinality sensitivity but only 9.52% of median activation energy; magnitude-normalized causal subspace actuation converts this mismatch into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy on untouched procedural data by +8.00 pp. Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation (MEA) reaches 81.25% of oracle targets versus 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched step budgets. With target and gate frozen before evaluation, targeted MEA improves the previous frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% on a new natural Stage-2 cohort (N=630; paired p=4.63e-7) and yields 65.741% versus 65.153% over all 7,992 examples while editing only 63 inputs. Prospective routing, replication across heads and models, and comparisons with attribution-steering baselines further characterize each stage, separating localization, actuation, reachability, target quality, and selective deployment as distinct control problems.

papers.title: One Sequence Is Enough: Fingerprinting Language Models from Fixed-Length Integer Sequences
papers.abstract: Users of model APIs and third-party platforms often rely on the declared model name to identify the model responding to their requests. However, the actual model may differ from the declared one, motivating identity verification based on observable outputs. Previous studies have shown that preferences in simple numerical-choice tasks can serve as model fingerprints. We investigate whether a single fixed-length integer sequence can combine multiple numerical observations to identify its source model. For this task, we introduce NumPrint, a benchmark of 5,036 answers from 51 models, collected using Chinese, Japanese, and English prompts that request 294 integers between 1 and 355 in one response. We propose the Shallow MLP and Causal Transformer (SMCT) to capture aggregate numerical preferences and behavioral patterns in generated sequences. In 51-class closed-set evaluation, SMCT achieves 92.72% accuracy from a single sequence, outperforming all methods compared in this study. Using two and four answers increases accuracy to 96.06% and 97.12%, respectively. These results show that a single integer sequence contains useful model fingerprints and that additional answers further improve identification.

papers.title: Beyond Fluent Responses: Finding User Dissatisfaction in Human-AI Interactions
papers.abstract: As large language models generate increasingly high-quality responses, recent work on response evaluation has moved beyond response-centered criteria, such as correctness and coherence, toward user-centered criteria, including user preferences and perceived usefulness. This shift is fundamentally important for developing technologies that are truly useful to real-world users. While conventional response evaluation quantifies the quality of the response itself, users' satisfaction in real conversations also depends on their subjective preferences and perceptions of usefulness, which do not necessarily align with response quality. This study investigates whether such user-centered signals can be detected from conversational text. Specifically, we analyze user utterances with self-reported dissatisfaction labels to examine whether user dissatisfaction in text can be detected. In English interaction, models using user utterances exceeded the 17.8% dissatisfaction label prevalence in AUPRC by up to 15 percentage points. These results suggest that user utterances reveal cues to implicit dissatisfaction. Furthermore, changes from the immediately preceding user utterance may improve dissatisfaction detection, with anomaly detection methods appearing particularly effective.

papers.title: IFRS Compliance Verification: An Open Multi-LLM Benchmark and Content-Conditioned Ensemble Classifier
papers.abstract: Verifying corporate financial disclosures against the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) is a core auditing task in which experts cross-reference disclosures with hundreds of fine-grained regulatory paragraphs: a laborious, costly, and error-prone process that motivates growing interest in large language models (LLMs) as compliance assistants. Yet single-model accuracy remains insufficient for high-stakes use, and naive ensembling is vulnerable to systematic per-model biases that can drag aggregate accuracy below that of the strongest individual annotator. This gap is addressed with a multi-stage framework, supported by a new benchmark of 19,998 IFRS regulation-disclosure pairs comprising 11,161 unanimous multi-LLM labels and 8,837 human annotations on items where the LLMs disagreed. The framework couples a three-stage domain-adapted sentence embedding pipeline (BERT masked language modeling on SEC EDGAR filings, unsupervised TSDAE and SimCSE adaptation, and supervised contrastive alignment) with a learned ensemble classifier that fuses frozen embeddings and LLM probability features from GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro via Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) optimized gradient-boosted trees. On the disagreement set, the ensemble achieves 81.7% weighted F1, exceeding the strongest single LLM by 10.4 points and majority voting by 14.6 points, and outperforms eleven unsupervised aggregation baselines; the retrieval pipeline attains Recall@15 of 45.3% on unseen regulations. The dataset, model checkpoints, annotation platform, and classifier implementation will be publicly released.

papers.title: PneuGen: Task-Driven Agentic Co-Design of Soft Pneumatic Robots
papers.abstract: Task-driven design of soft robots requires the consideration of factors such as geometry, morphology, material properties, and actuation, resulting in a large and complex design space that is challenging to explore. Computational optimisation methods leverage signals from simulation to iteratively improve designs to achieve task objectives. However, these methods typically demand high computational load for both optimisation and simulation. We present PneuGen, an agentic co-design framework for soft robots that leverages Large Language Model (LLM) agents to search over the soft robot design space efficiently. A designer agent proposes design programs from a parametric component library, and a separate critic agent analyses simulation diagnostics and recommends targeted revisions. Fitted module response models provide reusable physical priors relating geometry and pressure to deformation. Design programs are automatically validated and converted into finite-element simulations, enabling iterative evaluation. Across grasping tasks on primitive shapes and challenging objects, as well as shape-matching tasks that require multi-directional planar and 3D deformation, the proposed framework significantly outperforms prior computational optimisation baselines. Ablation experiments also highlight the utility of the critic agent and the module response model in facilitating efficient design. We additionally demonstrate the agent-generated soft robot designs in real-world shape-matching and grasping tasks.

papers.title: Catch It Where It Happens: Real Time Error Correction During LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.

papers.title: One Temperature to Rule Them All?
papers.abstract: Inference-time sampling is a central mechanism for improving large language models, with temperature controlling the tradeoff between reliability and diversity. While recent work suggests that varying temperature across samples can improve multi-sample inference, simple fixed-temperature schemes remain the standard in practice. We investigate this discrepancy in the canonical pass@K setting, asking when temperature diversity is useful, and when a single tuned temperature suffices. To this end, we analyze per-question success probabilities across multiple models and datasets, tracking how they vary with sampling temperature. We identify several consistent properties of these profiles, including that harder questions are less likely to share efficient sampling temperatures, although this trend is only logarithmic in hardness. We then derive an efficient method for evaluating the theoretically optimal multi-temperature allocation scheme, and show that although such a scheme improves performance, its gains over single-temperature baselines are typically modest when temperature is tuned as a function of the sampling budget K. We explain this phenomenon through mathematical mechanisms that we call dulling effects, and show how they ensure the robustness of temperature choices across different question distributions. Our results clarify when multi-temperature sampling is useful, and how temperatures should ideally be chosen.

papers.title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.
